In the previous video, you explored the first half of the evaluation
process, analyzing the agent's behavior, building test cases,
and defining criteria for judging the results.
Now in this video, you'll explore the second half of this overview.

Here, your goal is to measure how well the agent performs
and use those findings to guide improvements.

So, how do you turn those test cases and criteria into
evidence that you can use?

You start with evaluators, which check the agent's responses
and actions against your criteria.

To do that, you run the agent on your test cases and record its
responses and actions.

Some checks also need supporting information, such as the records
that the agent used.

You can review the results yourself or work with someone who
understands the task.

But reviewing every result takes time, especially when you keep
testing after changes.

Code evaluators and LLM judges let you automate some of that work.
Use code when you can write an explicit rule to make the check.

For Northwind, a code evaluator could compare the recommended product
and requested size with the stock records, then return a pass or fail.

Other checks require interpretation. For example,
do those clothes suit a winter camping trip?

You can use an LLM to assess the recommendation using your rubric,
the customer's request, and relevant product information.

When an LLM evaluates results this way, it's called an LLM judge.
You can implement both types of evaluator in your own Python code.

An evaluation platform can help you run the checks
and organize the results,
but you don't need a particular platform to use these methods.

In these examples, we'll be using Phoenix,
an open-source solution from Arize.

But before you rely on these evaluators, you need to check
that they're making the right judgments.

They can miss failures or flag acceptable results,
which could mislead you about what needs improving.

So compare their judgments with human judgments of the same results
using the same criteria and investigate disagreements.
The reviewer or the criteria may need correcting too.

You can then bring those individual judgments together to see how well
the agent performs across your evaluation set.

Once you have evaluators that can judge the agent's work,
you need to find out how consistently it meets your requirements.

An LLM can handle a request correctly on one run and fail on another,
even with the same input.
And it may handle some kinds of requests while struggling with others.

So a few successful responses aren't enough to establish
that it does the job reliably.

That's why you measure performance across different
cases and repeated runs.

Metrics, such as how often a requirement is met, help you understand
how consistently the agent performs in the situations you've tested,
and where it needs attention.

You can use those measurements to decide where to focus your efforts
and check whether your changes actually help.

You'll explore the practical methods in the later modules,
starting with building and testing evaluators in Module 3.

That brings you to the fourth and final part of the evaluation
process: using what you've learned to improve the agent.
You're going to want to first decide what needs attention.

Your results help you identify problems,
but how often something fails isn't the only consideration.

A less common mistake might matter more because of the
harm it could cause.

Improvement can also mean adding a capability or reducing cost
while keeping the quality you need.
Then, investigate the problem before deciding what to change.

Different problems call for different fixes,
so you want your changes to address what's actually going wrong.

For example, if Northwind gives product advice that isn't
supported by its catalog,

you might discover that its instructions never required it to stick
to that information.
Adding that requirement would be one change to try.

Other problems might call for better information,
changes to the tools or workflow, or a different model.

You're using what you found to decide what to change,
rather than trying fixes without understanding the problem.
But making that change doesn't establish that it worked.

You still need to test whether it improved performance and whether
anything else got worse.

To find out, you compare the original agent with the
version you changed.

You run both on the same test cases, and judge them using the same
criteria and evaluators.

That way, you're comparing their performance without also
changing how you measure it.

You want to check whether the problem you targeted has improved, but
also whether the agent still does the work it was already doing well.

A change can help in one situation and cause problems in another.
That loss of previously working behavior is called a regression.

For Northwind, the new instruction might reduce
unsupported product advice,

but also lead to unnecessary tool calls and make responses
slower or more expensive.

So you need to look at what got better and what got worse
before deciding whether the change is worth keeping.

That comparison helps you decide whether to keep the change,
revise it, or try something else.

And you still need to consider whether the results meet your
requirements. Better than before doesn't necessarily mean good enough.

If the evidence is unclear, you may need more testing before making
that decision. That concludes this overview of the evaluation process.
As you test the agent and see how it handles real requests,

you'll discover problems that lead to further improvements
and new things to evaluate.

You'll explore the details of this process throughout the course,
starting in Module 2.

But before you can put this process into practice,
you need evidence of what the agent actually did.

The final output won't necessarily show you which information it used,
which tools it called, or whether it skipped something important.

Traces record those steps so you can examine them and check whether
the agent did what it was supposed to do.

So you'll wrap up this module with a look at traces and how they give
you the evidence you need for evaluation.
